attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his published remarks, framed with 'I think' as his view. Not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: Captures the core claim that the field assumed prediction is enough for all of intelligence. Dropping 'fundamental' leaves out a judgment about importance but keeps the empirical content. 'I think' frames an opinion rather than a probabilistic hedge.

contract.note: The plain reading splits the claim into broad acceptance of the assumption and its inadequacy, which is fair. Using October 2026 for a 'has made' claim was the evaluator's choice. 'The field' and 'all of intelligence' are undefined, so the interpretation shapes the result.

evidence.note: A 2024/2025 preprint challenging next-token prediction. It shows debate exists but does not measure how widely the field holds the assumption in October 2026, or whether prediction is sufficient.

reviews.rationale: The only item is an older preprint that shows the paradigm is contested. It does not establish that the field broadly accepts prediction as sufficient, and it does not settle whether prediction is in fact insufficient. The packet does not decide the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus restates Pisano's point in his own words and explicitly agrees with it ('I agree... that'), so he has adopted it as his own claim.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the core observation that much discussion treats the current path as inevitable. 'Far too much' carries a normative judgment that cannot be scored, and the contract correctly sets it aside.

contract.note: Testing prevalence in October 2026 discourse is a reasonable plain reading. The population, scope, and meaning of 'path' are unspecified, so the evaluator's choices shape the result.

evidence.note: An October 2025 paper describing inevitability framing of AI adoption. It covers the wrong period and concerns adoption rather than a single development path, and it is not a representative measure.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence is a paper from a year earlier about framing AI adoption as inevitable. It does not measure how common single-path assumptions were in October 2026 discussion, so the packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his published remarks.

semantics.note: The sentence combines a normative prohibition with a causal claim ('suffering because... allowing'). Only the causal part is checkable and it is what the contract scores, so labelling the kind 'normative' misstates the scored claim.

contract.note: Scoring the causal harm claim and setting aside the prohibition is reasonable. The reading of 'unlimited access' as broad rather than literal is ordinary. The victims, the harm, and the October window were all supplied by the evaluator.

evidence.note: Wikimedia, as an affected party, reports ongoing costs and cleanup of AI-agent activity in October 2026. The costs are combined with general bot traffic and are not traced to the agents' broad internet access.
French official report on the October 11–12 refrigeration attack, attributed to an Iranian unit. It shows no AI-agent involvement, so under the contract it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Wikimedia suggests some agent-related burden in October but does not separate it from bot traffic or link it to the access configuration. The refrigeration attack shows no agent involvement. No investigation in the packet establishes the full causal chain the contract requires, and none refutes it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. In context, 'it' refers to large language models.

semantics.note: 'I think' states his view and is not a graded-confidence hedge. The proposition faithfully renders the claim that current LLMs reason very poorly.

contract.note: Judging current LLMs by leading October 2026 models on substantive reasoning tasks is an ordinary, fair reading of a general claim about current technology. The contract distinguishes results that rely on a harness from direct model tests.

evidence.note: Independent ARC Prize results from October 13: Gemini 4 Argon scores 98.5% on ARC-AGI-1 and about 91% on ARC-AGI-2, without the harness that the ARC-AGI-3 runs used. These are strong abstract-reasoning results.
Independent October 27 index: leading models score 78% on HLE-Diamond reasoning questions and up to 72% on a private set of hard physics questions. That physics test used a sandbox and a harness.

Expert-graded research mathematics, tested October 2–5: GPT-6 Astra, tested directly, solved 7 of 10 problems. Weak citations and exposition, plus the open-weight system's failures, are real limits but do not make performance very poor.
Shows a human–model gap on analogical reasoning, but tests older-generation models, so it does not describe the October frontier.

reviews.rationale: Three independent October 2026 evaluations show leading LLMs performing strongly on abstract reasoning, hard reasoning questions, and research mathematics. Some of these results come from direct model tests. Remaining weaknesses and the older-model gap in e4 do not support calling current reasoning very poor in general.
